The real problem is that a hash is only trustworthy as an identifier when the server itself proves hash equals SHA-256 of the query at registration — here the register endpoint just does store.set(hash, query) on raw client input, completely bypassing Apollo's built-in verification. Since nothing checks that the hash matches the query, an attacker can register their own query under a hash the real app already sends hash-only, and every subsequent hash-only call from legitimate clients would then execute the attacker's query — that's remote injection. The fix is to recompute sha256(query) on every write and reject mismatches with a 4xx, or better, ship a build-time trusted-documents manifest so clients never register at all. I'd also note the store is an unbounded Map with no TTL, so it grows forever. I'd verify by testing rejected mismatches, a working legit round trip, and that junk entries can't evict a known-good mapping.

A batching loader only collapses keys registered within the same event-loop tick — once that window closes, any later load() call opens a fresh one. Here the code awaits load() inside a for...of loop, so each iteration pauses until that promise resolves and the next load() lands on a later tick, closing the batch window after exactly one key every time. That's why the data-source log shows N single-key IN queries instead of one combined query — it's N+1 in disguise, and the loader's config and scope are fine, the bug is purely in the calling code's control flow. The whole point of APQ is amortization — after a one-time round trip where the client registers the full query and gets a hash back, every later call just sends the 64-character hash. But that only pays off if a hash means the same thing everywhere, and here the store is a plain Map living in one process's heap, so a hash learned on one replica is invisible to the other three. With round-robin routing across 4 replicas, a registered hash is only recognized about 1 in 4 times, which is exactly the ~75% miss rate we're seeing — and a rolling restart wipes a replica's Map entirely, causing a fresh miss storm. The fix is to match the storage to the deployment unit: Apollo's persistedQueries.cache just needs any object with get/set/delete, so swapping in something like RedisCache with a TTL makes registrations visible fleet-wide and survive restarts. For first-party clients, a build-time trusted-documents manifest goes further and removes the open registration surface entirely. I'd verify by watching the not-found rate drop near zero, payload shrink to hash size, a rolling-restart soak test pass, and load-testing the Redis hop itself.

DataLoader's contract is strict: the batch function has to return a results array the exact same length and order as the keys it was given, because DataLoader maps result[i] back to whoever called load(keys[i]) purely by index. Here the batch function groups by iterating the SQL rows instead of the keys array, and since an IN clause doesn't guarantee rows come back in the order you passed the ids, the output ends up ordered however the database happened to return rows. Worse, an author with zero books doesn't get its own group at all, so it silently deletes a slot and shifts every author after it by one index. The query itself is fine — this is purely a reshaping bug. It's intermittent because it only shows up when the DB's row order diverges from the key order or a zero-books author is in the mix, and a single-author test never catches it since there's nothing to be out of order relative to. The fix is to build a map keyed by id while iterating rows, then map over the original keys array and look each one up, defaulting to empty array. To verify, I'd assert every child's FK matches its parent and add a fixture with a zero-row entity sandwiched between two that have rows.

new PubSub() from graphql-subscriptions is entirely in-process — publish() only reaches asyncIterators that were created inside that same running Node process. On a single dev instance that's fine, there's only one process so mutation and subscription are always the same object and delivery is guaranteed. But with 3 replicas behind a load balancer, each one boots its own private PubSub instance, so you effectively have three separate topics that just happen to share a name. A subscriber's WebSocket is pinned to whichever replica accepted the upgrade, but each createPost mutation is a separate request the load balancer can route to any of the three independently. An event only reaches a subscriber when the mutation happened to land on the same replica the subscriber is connected to, which with uniform routing across 3 replicas is about 1 in 3 — exactly matching the reported symptom. Sticky sessions don't fix this, because they only pin the subscriber's connection, not the mutation requests. The real fix is swapping in something like RedisPubSub so publish and every replica's asyncIterator all read and write the same external topic. I'd verify by running 2+ instances locally, subscribing on one and mutating on the other, and confirming every event arrives exactly once.

First, the merge logic uses `??`, which can't tell the difference between a field that's omitted and one sent as explicit null — both are nullish, so `input.publishedYear ?? existing.publishedYear` always falls back to the old value. That means a client can never actually clear publishedYear, even though it's nullable specifically so it can be cleared. The fix is to branch on key presence instead of value — check `'publishedYear' in input` — so an omitted key leaves it untouched but a present key, including explicit null, overwrites. Second, archiveBook mutates the store but is registered under @Query instead of @Mutation, so the engine is allowed to parallelize or re-execute it, letting the side effect fire more than once or race with another field. Switching it to @Mutation restores serial execution. I'd add regression tests for null persisting, omitted preserving the old value, and calling the query field twice leaving state unchanged.

There are two separate bugs stacked here. The refund guard checks each incoming amount against the full captured total in isolation, without subtracting refunds that already succeeded — so three sequential refunds each for 60% of the captured amount all pass individually, and the order ends up refunded 180% against only 100% captured. The fix is to recompute remaining-refundable as captured minus the sum of already-succeeded refunds from the ledger on every request. Separately, the idempotency key is only checked at the service layer, so if the process crashes after the gateway call succeeds but before the key gets persisted, a retry won't find the key and will hit the gateway again as a brand-new refund. Forwarding the same idempotency key to the gateway call closes that gap, because the gateway's own idempotency map recognizes the repeat and returns the original result — you really need both layers guarded, since money operations over HTTP aren't retry-safe by default and each guard only covers its own boundary. The core issue is that the handler does the confirmation email and fulfillment notification synchronously before responding, which pushes total handler time past the gateway's delivery timeout. Since webhook delivery is at-least-once, the gateway reads that missed timeout as a failure and redelivers the same event — and each redelivery re-enters that same slow path, adding more load onto an endpoint that's already struggling, so rising p99 and duplicate deliveries are really one feedback loop, not two separate symptoms. An idempotency check by event id stops the ledger transition from being reapplied, but it doesn't stop a retry from repaying the cost of the slow email and fulfillment calls or occupying another request slot, so dedup alone can't stop the storm. The fix is to keep only signature verification, the idempotency check, and durably applying the ledger transition on the synchronous path, deferring the email and fulfillment notification to run after the 200 via a queue. But the 200 can only go out after the ledger transition is durably persisted — acking first and persisting second opens a crash window where the event is lost forever, since the gateway won't redeliver after a 2xx. The contract that makes deferring safe is that the gateway only needs confirmation the event was received and durably stored, not fully processed end to end. I'd verify by checking p99 ack latency under load, chaos-testing duplicate deliveries to confirm the transition applies exactly once, and killing the process between ack and the deferred job to confirm the work resumes instead of getting silently dropped.

The root cause is that @Body() only hands you the payload after NestJS's body-parsing pipe has already turned the raw request into a JS object, so by the time the controller sees it, the original wire bytes are gone. Re-serializing that object with JSON.stringify() isn't guaranteed to reproduce the exact bytes the sender transmitted — key order, number formatting, whitespace can all differ. Since an HMAC is computed over one specific byte sequence, hashing a re-serialized version produces a different message and a mismatching signature even when the payload is logically identical. That's also why the hand-written test script passes — it signs JSON.stringify(payload) and sends that exact string as the body, so the hashed and transmitted strings are identical by construction, which proves nothing about the real verification logic. And because the mismatch depends on incidental serialization differences that vary per payload, failures show up as intermittent and unpredictable in production even though the cause is fully deterministic. The fix is to capture the raw unparsed body — NestJS's rawBody: true option — and verify the signature against that Buffer before ever parsing into a DTO via @Body(). I'd test this with a captured genuine webhook replayed byte-for-byte expecting success, a single flipped byte expecting rejection, and a payload with deliberately reordered keys to prove verification no longer depends on re-serialization.

A webhook handler can only trust a confirmation once it proves four things: the source is genuinely the gateway via signature, the reference maps to a real order, the order is still in a capturable non-terminal state, and the transferred amount actually matches what's owed. This handler checks signature and reference but skips the last two. Missing the amount check is a real exploit — a transfer for less than the order total with the right reference still marks it fully paid. If the amounts don't match, the right move is to leave the order matched but still pending for reconciliation, not reject the event and not mark it paid. Delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once, so without a terminal-state check, a retried webhook re-applies the same transition — and once there's any side effect on that transition, like crediting a wallet or releasing inventory, a redelivered event becomes a double-credit or double-capture. Reviewing this is really about walking the guard chain and naming what's missing rather than commenting on style. I'd want tests proving an underpaid transfer stays pending, an exact-amount transfer marks paid, and delivering the same event twice results in exactly one transition.

A trustworthy webhook handler needs to check four things before acting: the signature actually came from the gateway, the reference maps to a real order, the order state, and that the amount matches. This one only checks signature and reference — it's missing the amount check, which means a transfer for less than what's owed but with the right reference could still get the order marked fully paid. It's also missing an idempotency check — webhook delivery is at-least-once, so if the same event gets redelivered, it'll try to apply the same transition again. My review would go check by check through what's present versus missing rather than nitpicking style. Before approving I'd want tests confirming an underpaid transfer doesn't wrongly mark paid, a correct-amount transfer does, and that delivering the same event twice only results in one state change.

It also doesn't guard against duplicate delivery; webhooks can be sent more than once for the same event, so without checking if the order's already been processed, a retry could re-trigger the same update.

Linking a new sign-in to an existing account by email only works when the provider returning that email is the same one that already verified it — a different provider reporting the same address is attacker-controlled and shouldn't be trusted as proof. The Google callback's email fallback is fine because Google verifies email before OAuth completes, but reusing that same lookup-by-email logic for GitHub carries an assumption that no longer holds there. The exploit is straightforward: an attacker registers a GitHub account with the victim's email, drives the callback, gets matched to the victim's row by email alone, has their githubId silently written onto it, and gets issued a session as the victim. A safer model matches on the stable provider id first and only treats email as an opt-in link key that requires the user to confirm while already authenticated. I'd also flag that gating the mock login purely on an env flag like MOCK_GITHUB isn't a real boundary — a leaked or misconfigured variable flips it on in prod, so it needs to be structurally excluded at build time. My review would name the actual broken contract — provider-id-first matching with email as a guarded link key — rather than commenting line by line. The fix: check githubId first like the Google flow, require confirmation for any email collision without a githubId match, gated on the provider's own email-verified claim. And I'd want tests for unverified or cross-provider email returning a pending-confirmation response instead of a token, repeat callbacks on the same githubId converging without duplicates, and a prod-config test proving the mock branch is unreachable.

I'd profile this rather than fix things in file order, since the three costs aren't equal — bcrypt's cost factor is exponential, so going from 10 to 15 is roughly 32x the hashing work, which alone probably explains most of the ~1s p95 regression. The thing is, that cost factor exists to make brute-forcing a low-entropy human password expensive; a refresh token is already a long random string, so hashing it at cost 15 buys nothing security-wise — I'd drop it back to the baseline of 10. Signing the access and refresh tokens has no dependency between the two calls, so awaiting them sequentially wastes time that Promise.all can reclaim. And RtStrategy.validate already loads the full user row while authenticating the caller, so refetching that same row by id in the service is a redundant round trip — I'd forward the validated user object through instead. None of this should touch the security invariants: the raw refresh token still never gets persisted, only its hash does, rotation still overwrites the stored hash, and a replayed old token still fails the compare and gets rejected. To verify, I'd measure p95 before and after on the refresh endpoint, run the existing behavioral suite, and check the query log shows one fewer findOne call per refresh.

JWT verification just confirms a token was signed with the right secret and hasn't expired — it doesn't tell you what type of token it is. issueTokenPair signs both the access and refresh tokens through the same jwtSecret() call, so they end up cryptographically indistinguishable apart from their exp claim. AtStrategy and RtStrategy both use secretOrKey: jwtSecret(), so a refresh token sails through the access strategy's check just like a real access token, since the payload is only { sub } with nothing encoding token type. The real root cause is the shared signing secret, not a bug inside either validate() method. Because the refresh token lives for 7 days instead of 15 minutes, this silently widens the leak window from minutes to a full week. The fix is using two distinct secrets, one for access and one for refresh, so each strategy can only validate its own token type. As defense in depth I'd also add an explicit type claim to the payload and assert it inside validate(), so a future same-secret mistake wouldn't reopen this. To verify, I'd replay the exploit: refresh token gets 401 on a protected route, fresh access token still returns 200, and /auth/refresh rejects an access token — locked in as a regression test.

In NestJS, guards inside @UseGuards run strictly in the order they're listed, so @UseGuards(RolesGuard, JwtAuthGuard) actually runs RolesGuard first. The problem is RolesGuard reads req.user.role, but req.user only gets populated by JwtAuthGuard after it verifies the bearer token. So with this ordering req.user is undefined for literally every request, and the check '!role || !requiredRoles.includes(role)' evaluates to true unconditionally — meaning a valid admin token, a wrong-role token, and no token at all all collapse into the same 403. A request with no token never even reaches JwtAuthGuard, the guard that's supposed to return 401, because RolesGuard short-circuits first — so those two symptoms are really one misordering bug, not two separate ones. The underlying rule is authentication has to run before authorization, since authorization has nothing valid to compare against otherwise. The fix is swapping the order to @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard) so identity gets attached first. This also matters for client behavior — 401 means re-login, 403 means don't retry with the same credentials — and collapsing both into 403 can mislead retry logic. I'd verify with a three-call matrix: admin token returns 200, wrong-role token returns 403, no token returns 401, locked in as a regression test.

There's a few things stacked here. First, the secret is a hardcoded literal, "secret123", and once that's in source control anyone with repo or git history access can mint a valid signature for any user, including forging isAdmin: true — that needs to move to ConfigService or an env-backed secret manager, and because the value is already burned it needs to be rotated immediately, not just relocated. Second, a JWT is stateless — there's no server-side switch to kill it before exp — so a 30-day expiry means a single leaked token grants a full month of access with nothing the backend can do. Since tokens can't be revoked individually, access tokens should be short, minutes-scale, and longer sessions should live in a separate refresh token with its own revocation path. Third, JWT payloads are base64url-encoded, not encrypted, so anything packed in there — a bcrypt hash, an isAdmin flag — is plainly readable by anyone holding the token. The payload should carry the bare minimum, basically sub and exp, with everything else looked up server-side from the verified user id. Also, storing the access token in localStorage exposes it to theft by any XSS on the page, so it should move to an httpOnly, Secure cookie. For the review, I'd rank these by real consequence rather than file order, pair each with a concrete fix, and call out what's already done right — the password comparison does use bcrypt before issuing a token. To prove it, I'd base64url-decode a real issued token to show the leaked fields directly, and codify the fix as a CI check that the secret always comes from env, plus a test asserting exp matches the intended policy.

The core problem is that clients should only ever see a message once it's actually committed to the database, and here the broadcast fires before the save even completes — that inverts the invariant and it's a real design defect, not just style. If saveMessage then rejects, say a constraint violation or the DB being down, no row ever gets written, so a refresh or a replay-on-join read shows nothing — every client in the room just watched a message that never actually existed. On top of that, saveMessage is called without await, so its promise is just floating — a rejection becomes an invisible unhandled rejection unless it eventually crashes the process. The broadcast payload is also built from the raw incoming body instead of the saved row, so it never carries the database-assigned id or createdAt, meaning there's no stable key for ordering or later pagination. The fix is to await saveMessage first, build the broadcast from the committed row's fields, and let a rejected save throw so the sender's ack surfaces the error while the room sees nothing. This does add the write's latency in front of the fanout, but that's worth paying — correctness matters more than shaving a few milliseconds. If async throughput is genuinely needed later, the right pattern is an outbox table or a queue that only broadcasts after the write is durable, not an optimistic emit. To verify, I'd write a failure-injection test that forces saveMessage to reject and assert zero sockets receive a broadcast while the sender's ack carries an error, paired with a happy-path test asserting the broadcast id matches the persisted row.

The volume here scales multiplicatively — keystrokes per second per typist times room size minus one receivers times number of concurrent typists — so a single 60-WPM typist alone produces roughly 5 emits a second, fanning out to about 199 sockets in a 200-person room, which is on the order of a thousand frames a second from just one person. Neither the client's per-keystroke emit nor the gateway's relay is actually broken code — the cost comes from tying emit frequency to keystroke rate instead of to the signal's real granularity. A typing indicator is ephemeral and lossy-tolerant — the receiver already fades it on its own after about 1.5 seconds with no new event, so its true resolution is 'once per fade window,' not once per keystroke, and anything faster is pure waste. The fix belongs on the client, at the emit source, since that's the cheapest point to cut volume before it even reaches the server's fanout. Specifically, a leading-edge throttle keyed to the fade window — emit immediately on the first keystroke of a burst, then suppress until the fade duration elapses. This preserves the UX exactly, because the receiver's fade timer resets on any emit within the window, so the appear-then-fade behavior looks identical with far less traffic. Typing state stays unpersisted, so there's no persistence tradeoff here, just the emit-frequency problem. A per-connection server-side rate limit is a reasonable defense-in-depth backstop but not where the real savings come from. To verify, I'd run a load test measuring relayed frames per second before and after under simulated multi-typist load, plus a two-client UX test confirming the indicator still appears promptly on the first keystroke and fades about 1.5 seconds after the last one.

So there are actually two bugs here that are really the same underlying issue viewed from opposite ends of a log. On the write side, `append` hands out a monotonic sequence number but never trims the room's array, so every room's history grows forever in memory. On the read side, `replaySince` filters everything newer than `lastSeq` with no cap, so a client offline for hours gets dumped one giant payload that freezes the page. Fixing only one side isn't enough — I'd add a ring buffer that shifts out the oldest entry once we hit a size cap, bounding memory, and also slice the replay result so payloads stay bounded regardless of offline duration. The honest tradeoff is that once a client's `lastSeq` falls outside the retained window, we can't reconstruct that gap from memory anymore — those messages are gone. If we need to survive past that horizon, history should live in Postgres, reusing `seq` as a pagination cursor for a 'load older' fetch, with the ring buffer just acting as a fast cache. I'd size the cap off real traffic — message rate times the offline duration we want to tolerate — not a guess. And I'd verify with a soak test confirming per-room memory plateaus at the cap, plus a long-offline reconnect test confirming the replay ack never exceeds the cap while still containing the newest messages.

The root cause is an off-by-one on the server: `replaySince` filters with `m.seq >= lastSeq`, which is inclusive, so it re-sends the exact message the client already has instead of starting after it. Since `lastSeq` means 'the last message I already have,' the comparison needs to be strictly greater-than. You can see it concretely — a client at `lastSeq: 4` reconnects, the inclusive filter returns `[4,5,6]`, and message 4 shows up twice because the client just appends `ack.messages` onto its existing list with no dedupe. Because `lastSeq` gets re-derived from the last item of each ack, this reproduces on every reconnect, so two blips compound into two duplicates. But fixing the operator alone isn't sufficient — with at-least-once delivery over a flaky connection, `replay-since` can legitimately fire twice for the same gap, so the client needs its own guard: track rendered messages by a composite key like `roomId:seq`, skip anything already seen, and only ever advance `lastSeq` forward with `Math.max`. There are three bugs here, and I'd rank them by severity. Most severe: the charge handler calls the gateway and records completion as two separate steps with no idempotency check between them, so if it crashes right after the gateway confirms but before completion is recorded, BullMQ retries the job and re-runs the charge from scratch — that's a real double-charge, actual money. The fix is using the payment id as the job id, which is already done, plus checking against previously processed payments before calling the gateway, or passing an idempotency key to the gateway itself. Second: `removeOnFail: true` discards the job's data as soon as it's marked failed, so by the time `onFailed` runs on the final attempt, `job.data` may already be gone and the dead-letter entry ends up empty or missing — that's silently losing exactly the data ops needs, so I'd set `removeOnFail: false` or a bounded retention window. Third, less severe: `onFailed` has no check on `attemptsMade` against the configured max, so it writes to the dead-letter queue on every failed attempt, not just the final one — attempts 1 or 2 are expected since a retry is coming, so this just produces noisy duplicate alerts rather than real harm. The fix is guarding with `job.attemptsMade >= (job.opts.attempts ?? 1)`. To verify, I'd want a forced-fail test showing exactly one dead-letter entry after the final attempt, a simulated mid-crash test showing exactly one charge after retry, and confirmation the dead-letter count stays flat while jobs are just retrying normally.

The problem is that every checkout uses the exact same lock key, `lock:inventory`, regardless of which SKU it's for — so a checkout on SKU A and one on SKU B end up contending for the same mutex even though they touch completely unrelated rows. Because the lock scope isn't tied to the resource being written, cluster-wide write throughput is capped by how fast one lock can be acquired and released, and adding more stateless replicas doesn't help since they all funnel through that same key. Both approaches trade a bit of extra complexity for parallelism — per-key locking needs a key or shard scheme, the atomic update pushes the complexity into interpreting a zero-rows result and retrying — but either removes the cross-SKU serialization. The actual bottleneck isn't the database or the network here; the replicas are already stateless and scaled out, it's the single shared lock key alone that's turning all their writes into a single-file queue. Nginx's default load-balancing algorithm is round-robin, which just picks the next backend by turn in the rotation — it has no visibility into whether that node is actually busy or idle. So a replica that's already stuck processing a heavy request still gets its next turn, and new requests keep piling onto an already-blocked node instead of being routed elsewhere. That matters a lot here because Node.js runs a single event loop per process, so a CPU-bound synchronous handler occupies that loop for its entire duration — no other request on that replica, not even something near-instant like /api/status, can be processed until it finishes. That turns one replica into a hot node: its queue and latency balloon under a burst of heavy calls while the other replicas sit comparatively idle. The underlying problem is really an algorithm-to-workload mismatch — round-robin assumes uniform, low-variance requests — rather than a logic bug in either handler. I'd fix it two ways: switch the load-balancing method to least_conn so new requests go to whichever backend currently has the fewest active connections, and offload the CPU-bound work to a worker_threads pool so the main event loop stays free to keep serving light requests concurrently. To validate, I'd send a mixed load of heavy and light requests through the load balancer and confirm latency spreads evenly across replicas with no single node's queue growing unbounded.

The replication is fire-and-forget — on failure we just log a warning, so an unreachable peer's write is never retried, and the two regions can permanently diverge instead of converging. Real eventual consistency needs a durable retry mechanism, like an outbox plus a background anti-entropy loop, not a catch that only logs. Worse, if both regions accept writes to the same account during a partition, reconnecting gives two different balances with nothing to resolve them — that's a missing conflict-resolution strategy. We'd need version numbers or vector clocks to detect the conflict and an explicit merge rule like last-write-wins or a CRDT, though naive LWW on money can silently lose or double-count funds. Choosing AP here should've been a deliberate trade-off — a CP design or a W+R>N quorum could preserve correctness. I'd flag the unretried writes and missing resolution as the real blocker, and verify by writing on both sides during a partition, reconnecting, and asserting the balance actually converges correctly.

There are really two separate problems here. First, the shard key is a RANGE key on createdAt, which is monotonically increasing, so every newly inserted document lands in the same last chunk — one shard absorbs almost all new-write traffic while the others sit idle. The balancer can rebalance existing chunks, but it can't fix a key that keeps generating new docs at one end forever, so this regenerates continuously — it's a design flaw, not something transient. Second, the maintenance job's updateMany filters on tier, a field the router has no chunk map for, so mongos can't target a single shard and instead broadcasts the write to every shard, each one scanning and locking its own slice — that gets worse as the cluster grows. Neither of these shows up in CI or a clean migration run, since they only manifest under real write volume. The real fix is resharding onto a hashed key, like hashed userId, or a compound key led by a high-cardinality field. Resharding is expensive and hard to reverse, so that's the actual review blocker, while the untargeted updateMany is a cheaper fix for later — it's fine if it's an intentional, called-out broadcast, but point-writes elsewhere should always filter on the shard key. The core problem is the leading wildcard — a LIKE '%keyword%' in SQL, or an unanchored $regex in Mongoose — which removes any fixed prefix an index could seek from, so neither the B-tree on name nor Mongo's default index can be used, and both fall back to scanning everything. That scan touches the whole table or collection on every call, so latency grows linearly with row count — you'd see Seq Scan with a huge Rows Removed by Filter in Postgres, or COLLSCAN with totalDocsExamined near the full collection size in Mongo. A plain B-tree only helps fixed-prefix patterns like LIKE 'keyword%' since it can jump to a known starting point in sorted order — it can't help here, and it's just adding write overhead for no read benefit. The real fix is a structure built for this: full-text search with tsvector plus a GIN index, pg_trgm for trigram substring matching, or something like Elasticsearch if we also need ranking or fuzzy matching. The core problem is that a feed is inherently per-user, but this code uses one shared key like feed:global for everyone, when it should be one ZSET per user keyed as feed:{userId}. That shared key also becomes a hotkey every read and write in the system hits, which defeats Redis Cluster's ability to spread load across hash slots — per-user keys would shard cleanly. Without a zremrangebyrank trim step after each zadd, the ZSET's size grows with the total post count of the whole platform forever, so memory and the cost of every zadd/zrevrange call climb unbounded; calling zremrangebyrank(key, 0, -(MAX+1)) right after each zadd would cap it. There are really two caching mistakes here. Setting s-maxage=31536000 with immutable tells shared caches to hold a response for a year and tells clients it'll never change, which only makes sense for a URL permanently bound to one piece of content, like a content-addressed or versioned key. A live playlist's payload mutates under the same key though, so applying that directive means the edge caches the first response and keeps serving that same stale segment list for up to a year with nothing to refresh it. The right approach for that kind of dynamic content is a short edge TTL, something like s-maxage=10, paired with stale-while-revalidate. The second issue is that when the handler throws something like NotFoundException instead of returning an explicit response, the resulting error carries no Cache-Control header, so the shared cache is free to apply its own default policy, and caching a 404 for an unknown key turns a transient miss into a sticky failure that every viewer at that cache keeps seeing. The origin should instead answer with an explicit short-TTL or no-store response. I'd lock this down with tests asserting the exact Cache-Control string per asset type, plus a test confirming unknown keys return a bounded, non-cached response.

ensureTranscoded only checks one thing, whether manifest.m3u8 already exists on disk, there's no lock or claim on the videoId before the ladder starts. Since that check and the encode aren't atomic, concurrent requests for the same cold video all see the file missing at once and each independently kicks off the full three-rung FFmpeg ladder, multiplying CPU by however many requests arrived together instead of costing one ladder per video, and those parallel runs also race to write the same output files, so whichever finishes last wins and the rest is wasted or corrupted. The fix is coalescing, not a bigger lock: keep an in-flight Map of videoId to Promise on the service, and after the existence check misses, look the id up there. If a promise is already in the map, await it and return, otherwise start the encode, store the promise synchronously before the first await, and remove it in a finally. It's the same shape as request-deduping or dataloader batching. An in-memory map only protects one process though, if this needs to work across instances it should move to a job queue like BullMQ keyed by videoId. Lazy transcoding is right as a default since most uploads are never watched, but it makes the first viewer wait out the whole ladder, whereas eager encoding on upload makes playback instant but burns CPU on clips nobody watches, so a middle ground is eager-encoding only content with a hot signal and keeping the lazy lock-protected path as fallback. I'd prove the fix worked by tracking how many ensureTranscoded calls actually reach the encode loop per cold videoId, which should drop from scaling with concurrency to a flat one, and by writing a test that fires many concurrent encode calls for one fresh video and asserts exactly one FFmpeg run produced one clean manifest.

Just because the PURGE call resolves without throwing doesn't mean anything got evicted — that only proves the HTTP request completed. NGINX here keys its cache purely on the request URI, but it still honors Vary: Accept-Encoding from the origin, so one URI can back multiple cached variants split by encoding. The purge call goes out through an HTTP client shared with other outbound requests, so it inherits that client's default Accept-Encoding header — gzip, deflate, br — even though a PURGE shouldn't carry one at all. When it does, NGINX tries to match one specific encoded variant, and if that doesn't line up with what's cached, it's a Vary mismatch and NGINX responds 412 instead of evicting anything. The handler doesn't help — it builds { purged: true } just from the request resolving, without ever checking the actual status NGINX returned. The origin only fires the verb; the edge decides whether anything's actually removed, so assuming success here means trusting a system we don't control. The real fix needs two parts: stop sending Accept-Encoding specifically on the PURGE call, and set proxy_ignore_headers Vary on the edge so it's one entry per URI regardless of encoding. To actually confirm a purge worked, I'd issue a fresh GET right after and check that X-Cache-Status flips to MISS, rather than trusting the handler's optimistic response.

That's not a one-off either — at any real failure rate it compounds and trends toward ENOSPC, where even healthy jobs start failing because there's no space left. The admit operation splits a read and a delete into two separate Redis round trips — ZRANGE then ZREM — so they're not atomic, and anything can happen in between. If two admit() calls run concurrently, both can read the same front-N slice before either's ZREM lands, so they end up removing the identical set of tokens — a classic read-then-remove race. That produces a double-admit: the same shopper token gets added to the admitted set twice, meaning one shopper gets into two concurrent checkout sessions, which cascades into oversell or double-charging downstream. The fix is replacing ZRANGE plus ZREM with a single ZPOPMIN call — since Redis is single-threaded, that collapses read-and-remove into one atomic command and no two callers can ever pop the same members. If we ever need extra logic like an inventory check before granting a slot, that has to go into a Lua script via EVAL so the whole thing stays atomic on the server rather than reintroducing the race. Separately, the admitted-tokens set never gets an EXPIRE, so a shopper who's admitted but abandons the flow leaves their token there forever, shrinking effective capacity over time even while the queue still has people waiting. The fix there is calling EXPIRE right after the SADD, sized to the real p99 checkout time, so abandoned grants recycle automatically. Of the two, the double-admit race is the more severe one since it breaks correctness directly, while the missing TTL is a slower degradation — I'd validate by firing concurrent admit() calls and asserting the token arrays are disjoint, and checking the admitted key has a positive TTL right after admission.

Calling zrange(0,-1) forces Redis to walk the entire skip list and serialize the full member list over the wire regardless of where the target sits, so that's O(N) on its own. Then doing indexOf on the client side is a second O(N) linear scan stacked on top, so one position lookup pays for two full passes. Since a sorted set already tracks order through a skip list, ZRANK can walk directly to a member's rank in O(log N) and return one integer—no need to transfer or scan the rest of the set. Swapping zrange+indexOf for zrank removes both costs at once, because the full list never leaves Redis in the first place. But the real driver of pain here is polling volume: a million waiters hitting this every few seconds is what saturates Redis CPU and bandwidth, not the algorithm alone. Wrapping the read-modify-write in a transaction only guarantees that the transaction's own writes commit or roll back together—it says nothing about whether another transaction can read or write the same row while the first is still running. Under the default Read Committed isolation, findOne without a lock option is just a snapshot read, so two concurrent transactions can both fetch the same stock value before either has written back. Both then subtract quantity from that same stale number and save, so the second write overwrites the first without any awareness of it—a classic lost update that lets the system oversell. Adding lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } makes TypeORM emit SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which forces a second transaction's read of that row to block until the first commits or rolls back. Once forced to wait, its read reflects the already-decremented stock, which serializes every decrement against that SKU and closes the lost-update window. Atomicity and serialized row access are genuinely separate guarantees—a transaction boundary alone gives you the former, not the latter. I'd also keep the locked section as small as possible—lock, check, subtract, insert, commit—since holding it longer just increases contention. To validate, I'd fire something like 200 concurrent decrement-by-1 calls against a seeded stock of 100 and confirm exactly 100 succeed, the rest fail with an insufficient-stock error, and the final stock floors at zero without going negative.

The current guard does a redis.get followed by a separate redis.set, and that gap between read and write is exactly the race the idempotency key was supposed to close—two concurrent requests can both read null before either has written, so both pass the check and both create an order. It's the same shape as a SELECT-then-INSERT race, just moved one layer over onto Redis. The fix is to collapse that into one atomic command: SET key PENDING EX 30 NX, so among any number of concurrent callers exactly one SET returns OK and everyone else gets null immediately. A caller that loses that race shouldn't just retry—it should GET the key and branch: if it's still PENDING, return a 409 telling the client to retry later; if it's a cached result, return that marked as a replay. I'd also keep a UNIQUE constraint on the idempotency key column at the database layer as a backstop, for cases like the TTL expiring mid-flight or a Redis flush wiping the claim. When that constraint fires as a 23505 error, the code should catch it, re-read the row by the key, and return it as a replay instead of letting a raw 500 through. I'd validate this with two concurrent requests sharing a key, confirming exactly one creates the order and the table ends up with exactly one row for that key.

Replaying a cached result without checking it against the incoming body means a client that reuses the same idempotency key with a different payload—say a changed order amount—silently gets back the old response instead of an error. The fix is to store a fingerprint, a SHA-256 hash of the request payload, alongside the cached result, then recompute and compare it on every replay lookup: a match replays safely, a mismatch should return 422 rather than replaying stale data or quietly processing it as unrelated. Separately, wrapping the Redis lock-acquisition call in a try/catch that returns 'ACQUIRED' on any error is fail-open—once Redis goes down, every concurrent request is treated as having won the lock, so the guard stops preventing duplicates for the whole outage. The correct posture is fail-closed: if the lock store is unavailable, the operation should reject with something like 503 rather than proceed as if the guard succeeded. A database UNIQUE constraint is a valid last resort, but only if the app actually catches the unique-violation error—left uncaught, a legitimate concurrent retry crashes with a raw 500 instead of getting back the successful result. Handling it correctly means re-fetching the persisted row by key and returning it as a replay, matching the same behavior as the cache path. Together this is defense-in-depth: cache for speed, DB constraint for durability, fingerprint for distinguishing a real retry from a different operation reusing the same key. I'd flag the silent-corruption and fail-open issues first since they have the biggest blast radius, and test: same key with a changed body returns 422, store-down still yields one record via the DB constraint, and a racing retry replays instead of 500.

This is a classic check-then-set race. Reading the lock key and then writing it are two separate round trips, so there's a window where a second caller can read 'no lock' before the first caller's write has landed — concretely, two ride requests resolving to the same nearest driver can both call redis.get and see nothing locked before either one calls redis.set, so both fall through the guard and both remove the driver from the geo set, double-booking them. It's a textbook TOCTOU: the vulnerability is in the gap between check and use, not in Redis itself, since each individual command is atomic but the pair isn't. The fix is replacing that GET-then-SET with a single SET key value NX call, which is atomic — of several concurrent NX writes racing on the same key, exactly one succeeds and the rest return null. Only the request that wins the lock should remove the driver from the pool; a loser should fall through to the next candidate in the ring instead of erroring. Separately, the lock key needs a TTL, because without one, a process that crashes after winning the lock but before confirming the trip leaves that driver stuck forever. The order matters too — acquire the lock first, then remove from the pool, so a losing request never removes a driver it doesn't own. And since this only shows up under real concurrency, I'd verify it by firing simultaneous requests at the same driver and asserting exactly one succeeds, ideally also confirming the old check-then-set version fails that same test as a negative control.

The core issue is that every mutation re-serializes the entire index to JSON, so write cost scales with total index size instead of with the size of the change — that's write amplification, and it means throughput collapses under high-ingest load even though each individual write is tiny, because CPU in JSON.stringify and bytes written to Redis both grow with corpus size. The fix is to stop rewriting the full snapshot every time and instead persist just the delta, saving the full compacted write for a slower background schedule. One way is an append-only log — push a small {op, id, content} entry to a Redis stream per mutation, which is O(1), then periodically compact with a full serialize, and on boot replay the log on top of the last snapshot. An alternative is the Lucene segment model — each batch of mutations becomes a small immutable segment, a background job merges old ones, and boot reads all live segments. Either way you're trading simplicity for performance, taking on compaction, crash recovery, and tombstone handling — which is why full-snapshot writes are still a reasonable choice for a single-node, low-ingest, or teaching-scale service. It's really a decision driven by ingest rate and corpus size, not a correctness bug. I'd verify it by benchmarking write latency and CPU against corpus size before and after, and running a restart test to confirm the rebuilt index matches exactly.

It's worth being upfront that this is an approximation, not an exact count — you're trading a small, known error, something like 0.003% at reasonable traffic, for eliminating that O(N) memory blowup and the eviction cost on hot keys. Because of that, anything where the count itself is the source of truth — billing, hard quotas, audit trails — needs to stay on the exact ZSET log; only clients that are genuinely hot and can tolerate a small margin should move to the counter. Redis Cluster splits the keyspace into 16384 hash slots, computed as CRC16 of the whole key mod 16384. The three keys here — quota:u:<userId>, quota:t:<tenantId>, quota:g — share no common substring, so they almost certainly hash to different slots, possibly different nodes. The bug is that writeChunk takes the client-supplied sha256 field and uses it directly as the chunk's identity, for both the dedup lookup and the derived storage key, without ever recomputing the hash from the actual bytes received. That breaks the core invariant of content-addressable storage, where a key is supposed to always equal the hash of the bytes it points to — trusting a client-asserted value instead breaks that right at the boundary where untrusted input enters storage. If the claimed hash happens to collide with an existing dedup entry, the request is treated as a HIT and silently returns bytes for completely different content than what the client uploaded. If it doesn't exist yet, we insert a new dedup row keyed by that unverified hash, which poisons the index going forward — every future lookup inherits the corruption. It also means ordinary transit corruption goes undetected, since mangled bytes just get filed under whatever hash the client originally claimed. The fix is to recompute the digest server-side from the actual received bytes with createHash('sha256').update(data).digest('hex'), and only ever use that recomputed value for the dedup lookup and objectKeyFor — the client's claimedSha becomes just a verification assertion we compare against and reject with a 400 sha256_mismatch if it disagrees. More generally, any identity a client can freely name for data it also supplies has to be independently derived or verified server-side.

If it doesn't match anything, we insert a brand new dedup row under that unverified hash, which poisons the index for anyone who looks it up later. The bug is in how the last chunk gets built. Buffer.alloc(CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES) allocates a full zero-filled 1MB buffer, and copy only writes as many bytes as actually exist in the source range — for every full chunk that's fine since there's a full 1MB there, but for the file's final chunk the range runs past payload.length, so copy writes fewer real bytes and the rest of the buffer stays zero. Hashing that buffer means the last chunk's digest is actually sha256 of the real tail bytes plus zero padding, not sha256 of just the real bytes — the padding gets baked into the content-addressed hash. That breaks dedup, because those same real tail bytes stored anywhere else hash differently without the padding, so a lookup never matches. It also breaks integrity checks, since re-hashing the actually stored bytes correctly can never reproduce this padded digest, so a fine file gets flagged as corrupt. The core problem with storing the chunk manifest as a single JSONB array on the file row is that sha256 lives inside array elements rather than as a real column, so it's unindexable — a global dedup lookup for 'does this hash exist anywhere' degrades into scanning and parsing every file's array. Updating a single chunk means reading the whole array, mapping over it to change one element, and writing the whole thing back, so an N-chunk file rewrites all N entries just to change one — that's real write amplification, and it's not concurrency-safe either: two requests updating different chunks of the same file both read the array before either writes, so whichever finishes second silently overwrites the first with no error. On top of that, chunkCount as its own column drifts from the real chunks.length if any write path forgets to keep them in sync. The fix is a normalized file(1)->chunk(N) model with a ChunkEntity, a unique index on (fileId, chunkIndex), an index on sha256, and chunkCount derived from COUNT(*) instead of hand-carried. That said, JSONB is genuinely fine when you're just fetching the whole manifest for the client in one row read — the tradeoff only tips toward normalizing once existence and missing-chunk queries become the steady state. So the issue here is that we're storing the full HTML as a plain text column right inline with url, host, statusCode — so each row's size ends up dominated by the page body, not the small metadata fields. Once that text passes about 2KB, Postgres pushes it out-of-line into TOAST, which bloats the table and skews the planner's row-width stats. Because that bloat affects the whole table, even metadata-only queries like listing pages or looking up by host slow down, even though they never touch htmlBody. The fix is to push the raw HTML to object storage like S3 or MinIO under a key derived from a hash of the URL, and keep just a content digest plus that object key in the row. The digest is nice because it also lets us detect duplicate or unchanged pages without re-reading the full HTML every crawl. The write path still upserts the same small metadata row, but the body write goes through an object-storage put instead of populating htmlBody, so a metadata scan now hits small, fixed-width rows with no TOAST involved. To be clear, inline storage isn't wrong at small scale — it's fine for a demo. The trade-off only tips toward object storage at billions of rows, where the extra network hop to fetch the body plus the added consistency burden are worth it to keep the hot metadata table small and fast. I'd verify this by comparing metadata-query latency and table-plus-TOAST size before and after, and confirming the HTML is still retrievable end-to-end via its object key.

The bug is that enqueue does BF.EXISTS, BF.ADD, and zadd as three separate awaited Redis calls with no atomicity between them, so two workers can both check membership on a brand-new URL, both see a miss, and both push it onto the ZSET as a duplicate before either one has actually registered it in the bloom filter. On top of that correctness issue, each enqueue pays three sequential network round trips, and since each call has to finish before the next starts, that round-trip count directly caps how many URLs we can accept per second. The fix is to fuse all three into a single Lua script registered as a custom ioredis command via redis.defineCommand, since Redis executes a Lua script as one atomic, single-threaded operation. That means no second worker can ever observe the bloom filter mid-check, which closes the race entirely, and collapsing three round trips into one gets us roughly a 10x throughput improvement. That said, bloom-filter dedup is inherently best-effort anyway, so an occasional duplicate enqueue is usually harmless — this fix really matters when you need exactly-once enqueue semantics or you're throughput-bound on this path specifically. I'd verify correctness by hammering enqueue concurrently with the same new URL from many clients and checking the queue grows by exactly one, and verify the throughput claim by benchmarking enqueues-per-second before and after the change.

The root cause is that the enqueue path never calls BF.RESERVE before issuing BF.EXISTS or BF.ADD, so RedisBloom just auto-creates the seen:urls filter on the first bloom command it sees, using its own built-in defaults rather than anything we configured. Those defaults are roughly a 0.01 error rate and a capacity of exactly one hundred items, which is exactly why the frontier stalls right around the hundred-URL mark. Once real inserts exceed that reserved capacity, the actual false-positive rate climbs way past what's advertised, so BF.EXISTS starts telling us brand-new URLs are already seen and the crawler wrongly throws them away as duplicates. And because a bloom filter's only failure mode is the false positive, nothing throws or logs — it's normal behavior from Redis's point of view, so the frontier just silently stops accepting most URLs. The fix is to explicitly call BF.RESERVE with the real error rate and capacity on module init, or lazily right before the first enqueue, sizing capacity to about 1.5x the expected number of unique URLs for headroom. A dangling node is one with out-degree zero — no outlinks at all — so under the bare recurrence its rank mass has nowhere to flow. Looking at the loop, the inner accumulation only gathers rank from other nodes' inlinks; there's no separate step anywhere that collects a dangling node's rank and redistributes it back across the graph. Because that dangling mass never gets redistributed, the sum of the rank map drifts below 1 after every pass, and the ranking becomes unstable across iterations. The fix is to compute a danglingSum each iteration — the sum of rank over every node with zero out-degree — derive danglingShare as damping times danglingSum over N, and add that share to every node alongside the existing teleport term, so the vector re-normalizes back to summing to 1. A good regression test would assert the sum of rank values stays approximately 1 after every iteration on a graph that deliberately includes a dangling node. And honestly the missing piece is conceptually the same as the teleport term — both add a flat amount to every node per iteration — which is exactly why it's easy to overlook, since the code otherwise looks like a correct damped power iteration.

The SET NX PX plus Lua CAS renew only guarantees one active leader at any instant — it can't stop a paused process, say during a GC pause, from resuming and still holding isLeader=true even after a successor took its lease, because nothing notified it. If that stale leader then fires a non-idempotent write like a charge or a batch of emails, with no term or idempotency key, it can double-fire. I'd close that with a monotonic fencing token so downstream rejects a lower term, or make the write idempotent, keyed by something like jobDate:customerId, so a replay just no-ops. Separately, renewIntervalMs equal to leaseMs leaves no margin — one slow Redis call and you get a false failover; it should be a third of the lease or less. In review though, the unfenced side effect is the real blocker, the timing is just a nitpick — and I'd want a test that pauses a leader across a term boundary and checks downstream rejects the stale write.

If that resumed but no-longer-real leader then executes a non-idempotent write, like charging a customer or firing off emails, with no term attached, the same action can happen twice. I'd fix it by attaching a monotonic fencing token so the downstream system rejects any call carrying an older term than the last one it accepted. By default an etcd3 read is linearizable — it does a ReadIndex confirmation, so the leader checks with a majority via heartbeat before answering, no log write but you still pay roughly one leader round trip. Calling .serializable() skips that and answers from whatever replica got the request, basically free, but can lag the true state by tens of milliseconds — bounded staleness, not unbounded. The real split isn't how often a read happens, it's whether the read decides something — like who holds a lock or who's leader — versus just displays something like a dashboard count. A stale answer on a lock-owner read can hand the same lock to two callers, so that has to stay linearizable, while a dashboard being a few milliseconds behind is harmless and fine to switch to .serializable(). So the fix is routing per call, not a global downgrade — only the tolerant reads get switched. I'd prove the win with p99 latency measurements on both paths, and I'd lock in the routing rule with a test that spies on the lock-owner read's call and asserts .serializable() never gets chained onto it.

That said, sharding the key doesn't remove per-attempt overhead — every acquire, even a refused one, still pays the full cost of the parallel SET NX PX round trips across nodes plus the validity math. Separately, commandTimeout set almost equal to the TTL, like 900ms against a 1000ms TTL, leaves basically no headroom — one slow node eats nearly the whole TTL and validity comes out zero or negative, forcing a wasted re-acquire. None of this weakens correctness — you still need quorum to acquire and the fencing token still gets checked on every write. I'd validate the fix with a throughput test comparing the single global key against the sharded keys and confirm two workers never hold the lock for the same job id at once.

If a node misses its renewal window because of a blip, a follower can legitimately grab the key with SET NX PX, but the demoted node's next tick still calls pexpire on that same key and extends a TTL that now belongs to the new leader — so you get split brain, two replicas both believing isLeader is true and both running the leader job at once. This never shows up in a single-leader smoke test since on the happy path the value under the key never changes out from under the current leader. The fix is an atomic compare-and-swap, a Lua script that does a GET, compares it to this node's own id, and only calls PEXPIRE on a match, returning something like 0 on mismatch — Redis runs Lua single-threaded so that closes the race that exists when GET and PEXPIRE are two separate round trips. On a mismatch, the node should immediately set isLeader to false, log the step-down, and go back to competing for the key like any follower, instead of retrying the renew.

The usable lock window isn't the raw ttlMs you passed in, it's ttl minus however long acquisition itself took minus clock drift between the Redis nodes voting on it. Because the Promise.all over the per-node SET NX PX calls has no per-node timeout, one slow or dead node can stretch that acquisition time out to almost the full ttl before quorum resolves. But the code hardcodes validityMs to ttlMs instead of computing it from Date.now() captured before and after the parallel calls, so the reported validity is completely disconnected from what actually got consumed. The grant condition should be quorum reached AND validityMs greater than zero, not just quorum — when validity comes out zero or negative it needs to fail closed, releasing the lock everywhere and returning acquired:false, same as the existing quorum-miss branch. This bug is silent on the happy path because when nodes are healthy Promise.all resolves almost instantly, so even a correct calculation lands close to ttlMs anyway. But with, say, a 5 second ttl and one node taking 4800ms, the real remaining validity is more like 200ms minus drift, and the unfixed version still reports validityMs 5000 and acquired true — so a worker thinks it has five more seconds when it's basically already expired, letting a second worker grab the same resource. On top of fixing the calculation, ioredis should have commandTimeout and connectTimeout set to well under 10% of ttlMs so one dead node can't drag things out, and the critical section itself should stay under roughly 30% of the validity window.

If it's a materialized view instead of a hand-maintained table, you'd need a periodic job, like a NestJS @Cron(), to REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY. After the fix, GET /invariant becomes a single-row read, O(1) regardless of table size — which is actually the same write-through-cache pattern account.balance already uses, so only the global invariant check was still doing the expensive full recompute. The nightly scan is bottlenecked by two things at once — the sheer number of accounts, and the fact that there's only one worker draining the queue with concurrency=1, so no matter how fast any single query runs, that serial walk becomes the ceiling once we're at billions of accounts. This is architectural, not a slow-query problem. I'd fix it two ways, and they're complementary, not either-or. First, partition the account base — by id hash, country, whatever — into separate queues, each with its own worker, so partitions reconcile in parallel instead of one long serial walk. Second, add an activity-driven filter, like a CDC stream off the ledger table via Debezium or even LISTEN/NOTIFY, so a run skips accounts with no activity since the last cutoff instead of re-summing every account regardless of whether it changed. Partitioning alone still re-sums every untouched account within each partition, and filtering alone still funnels every matching account through one worker per partition, so you need both. I'd keep each partition's queue at concurrency=1 still, since that's what guarantees two workers never race on the same account and post duplicate compensating entries. I'd also anchor each run to a single cutoff timestamp captured at the start, rather than an open-ended 'now', so an in-flight transaction doesn't get mistaken for drift. The one risk with the CDC path is a dropped or missed event silently hiding real drift, so I'd still run a periodic full unfiltered sweep, maybe weekly, as a backstop to prove the filtered runs aren't missing anything.

The root cause is that I was taking row locks in whatever order the arguments arrived — fromAccountId first, then toAccountId — instead of a deterministic order, so the lock sequence ends up depending on transfer direction. When an A→B transfer and a concurrent B→A transfer both run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in opposite orders, A→B locks A and then blocks waiting on B, while B→A locks B and blocks waiting on A — that's a classic ABBA cycle. Postgres's deadlock detector spots that wait-for cycle and aborts one of the two transactions with a deadlock detected error while letting the other proceed, which is exactly why it shows up as an intermittent 500 instead of a hang. Single-direction transfers on a pair never hit this, since only opposite-direction concurrent transactions on the same pair actually form the cycle. The fix is to sort the two account ids and always lock the smaller one first, ideally as one query — SELECT ... FROM account WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE with a pre-sorted array. Once both directions are forced to grab the same first row, the second transaction just queues behind the first instead of racing into a cycle. This costs nothing for unrelated transfers either, since disjoint account pairs never contend on the same row, so full parallelism is preserved elsewhere. I'd verify by firing lots of concurrent A→B and B→A transfers on the same pair under load and confirming zero deadlock errors, correct final balances, and an intact SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT) invariant.

The issue is we only write the saga_step row after the HTTP call to wallet-service returns, on both success and failure. So for the whole duration of that call there's no row at all — the blind window is between wallet-service applying the debit and sagaSteps.save() actually running. If we crash there, recovery can't tell a step that never ran apart from one that ran but never got recorded, because both just look like a missing row. That ambiguity leaves recovery with no basis to resume or compensate, so a real debit can happen with nothing durable to show it. The fix is write-ahead: insert a 'started' row before calling wallet-service, then update it to ok or failed after. That makes the table, not the in-memory call() frame, the source of truth. A stuck 'started' row is exactly the signal recovery scans for, and it can then query wallet-service with sagaId plus step id as an idempotency key to decide whether to resume or compensate.

The core problem is that balances in minor units — cents, VND, satoshi — routinely exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER once an account gets large, and JavaScript's Number can't represent integers past that exactly. When we do Number(truthBalance) - Number(ledgerBalance), that coercion rounds to the nearest double once we cross the boundary, so the computed drift is off by whole units with zero warning. It gets worse because the endpoint returns drift as a JSON number, so even a correct backend value gets re-coerced a second time by any client that parses it. The write path has the same bug — parseAmount calls parseFloat(raw), so a large transfer can get rounded before it even reaches the ledger. This is dangerous specifically because it's silent: nothing throws, we just write a slightly-wrong compensating entry, and the double-entry invariant can drift for weeks unnoticed. The fix is to do all money arithmetic in BigInt, parsing with BigInt(raw) so bad input like '12.5' throws instead of truncating, and serialize every money field as a JSON string, not a number. I'd verify it by seeding a drift value above 2^53 and asserting both the drift and response are exact and stringified.

The Map lives in the heap of a single Node process — it never crosses a process boundary. Once we run multiple replicas, each one boots its own empty Map, so they end up with completely independent, disconnected views of circuit state for the same host. Concretely, if replica B racks up failures and flips its local entry to open, replica A's Map has no idea — A just keeps sending jobs to a host that's already known to be down. That defeats the whole point of a circuit breaker, which is supposed to protect the host, not one process's private view of it. On top of that, any deploy, crash, or scale-down wipes the heap, so all the breaker state — fail counts, openUntil — silently resets to closed with zero signal that a circuit was ever open. Really this state is inherently shared across replicas, so it belongs in something external like Redis. The fix is to delete the Map and keep the same four pieces — state, fails, a probe gate, and openUntil — as Redis keys per host, read and written through a shared client. A NX EX probe key acts as a single-probe gate so only one replica sends the half-open recovery probe at a time. I'd verify it by running two workers against the same Redis, tripping the breaker from instance A, then confirming instance B's allowRequest also returns false for that host.

Plain SELECT FOR UPDATE with no SKIP LOCKED takes row locks on the matched rows, so any other transaction running that same query has to wait for those locks instead of moving to different rows. That's exactly what happens with two poller replicas — the second one ends up blocked behind the first's lock on the same top-N rows, so they run serially, which is why throughput doesn't improve with a second replica. Adding SKIP LOCKED lets a poller skip rows already locked and claim the next available ones instead, so replicas partition the pending set into disjoint batches and actually run in parallel. The UPDATE to in_flight has to happen in the same transaction as the claiming SELECT, before commit, so a row is marked taken the instant it's claimed — that's what stops a later poller re-claiming it once locks release. But SKIP LOCKED is just a concurrency mechanism for a scalable queue — it fixes throughput and double-claiming, it's not an exactly-once guarantee. It doesn't cover a crash mid-delivery, so we still need a watchdog resetting stuck in_flight rows after a timeout plus an idempotency cache on the receiver. I'd verify by running multiple replicas concurrently and checking claimed-rows-per-second scales roughly linearly instead of flatlining, and confirm no row ID ever gets claimed by two replicas at once.

The UPDATE to in_flight needs to be in the same transaction as the SELECT, committed together, so nothing else can grab that row once it's claimed. Right now we compute the HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body and run the constant-time comparison before we even check the timestamp window, so every request pays for that crypto work regardless of whether it's going to be rejected anyway. Under a flood of stale or replayed requests, all of them are guaranteed to fail the window check, but we still do the full HMAC first — burning CPU on an outcome the clock already decided. The window check only needs the timestamp from the parsed header and the current clock, no secret and no crypto, so it's basically free by comparison. The fix is to move that check right after parsing the header, before calling sign() and constantTimeHexEqual, so stale requests get rejected without paying the crypto cost, while requests that pass still go through full verification. This is purely a cost change, not a behavior change — a stale timestamp was always rejected and a forged-but-in-window signature is still caught by the constant-time compare. Keeping constantTimeHexEqual for anything that passes the window check preserves the timing-attack resistance since only the ordering changes, not the comparison method. I'd verify by flooding the endpoint with out-of-window requests before and after — CPU and latency should scale with the flood before the fix and stay flat after — and also confirm valid in-window signed requests still succeed.

HMAC is computed over raw bytes, not JSON semantics — two logically identical objects can hash differently once serialized differently. On the sender we sign JSON.stringify(payload), but a later reformat step runs JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body), null, 2) before the actual POST, so we send different bytes than we signed. On the receiver, Nest's body parser already parsed the request before our handler runs, so re-stringifying req.body produces a third, independently-formatted string. Three different byte sequences can never match, secret or not — this is a serialization bug, not an auth failure. Fix: drop the sender's reformat step, and on the receiver enable rawBody:true and hash req.rawBody directly instead of req.body. I'd verify by resending and confirming 200, then diffing the signed bytes against the raw bytes received to prove byte-for-byte identity.

BullMQ counts every uncaught throw as a failed attempt unless the job was already rescheduled via moveToDelayed before that throw — a plain throw new Error('circuit open') looks identical to a real rejection from the receiver. During a sustained outage the circuit stays open across many delivery cycles for the same event, and each skipped cycle still burns an attempt, so after a few cool-downs attemptsMade hits 3 and the event lands in dead_letter even though the receiver never saw the request. The fix is ordering: await job.moveToDelayed(...) must run first, then throw new DelayedError() — that's BullMQ's explicit 'already handled' signal; thrown in the wrong order or as a plain Error, it still counts. This also matters for the half-open probe, which reuses the same path and needs the same protection. I'd verify by holding the circuit open across several cool-downs and confirming attemptsMade stays flat, with only receiver-rejected events reaching dead_letter.

Opening a DB transaction and then making the HTTP call before COMMIT stretches the transaction across the entire round-trip to the receiver. While it's open, the pooled connection is unavailable to other requests and the row locks from the preceding INSERTs stay held, so a slow or hanging receiver starves the whole connection pool even though the receiver has nothing to do with the database. Worse, tying commit success to the HTTP outcome reintroduces the exact send-then-commit dilemma outbox is supposed to avoid — a throw rolls back rows the receiver may have already acted on, or the process could crash after axios.post resolves but before COMMIT, leaving a delivered webhook for an order that never persisted. The fix is for publish() to only insert the order and a pending outbox_event row, then commit and return; a separate poller claims rows with SELECT...FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and does the POST outside any write-path transaction. I'd verify by killing the process right after the outbox commit and confirming the poller still delivers it on restart.

Calling subscribe on every chat:join re-issues a Redis SUBSCRIBE even when this node is already listening on that channel, which is redundant. And on disconnect we only tear down the Socket.IO room membership, leaving the Redis subscription in place, so the node keeps listening long after its last local member left. Without a per-room reference count there's no way to tell 'already subscribed, one more joined' from 'first member, need to subscribe' — so join blindly re-subscribes and leave never unsubscribes. That's not free: every message on a stale channel still arrives, gets parsed, and is discarded with zero local sockets to deliver to, and since rooms constantly empty and refill, the leak only grows over the node's lifetime. The fix is a Map<string, number> ref count — subscribe only on the 0->1 transition, unsubscribe only on 1->0. I'd verify with PUBSUB CHANNELS and NUMSUB right after the last member leaves a room.

Calling io.to(room).emit() once per incoming message puts the cost on the gateway's own event loop — a 50-message burst means 50 full encode-and-broadcast passes back to back. A RoomBatcher fixes this by decoupling arrival from delivery: enqueue() appends to a per-room buffer and arms a setTimeout, around 50ms, the moment the buffer goes from empty to non-empty; later messages in that window just ride the already-armed timer. When it fires, the buffer flushes once as a chat:batch emit, turning N calls into roughly ceil(N/maxSize). A maxSize cap forces an early flush under unbounded bursts, and the timer should be unref()'d so it never blocks shutdown, while still flushing on SIGTERM so nothing gets silently dropped. This trades up to one windowMs of latency — imperceptible for chat — for a big drop in operation count, with total bytes unchanged. I'd verify by flooding a room and confirming batch count is far smaller than message count while every message still arrives.

The bug is that Redis sizes a bitmap by the largest offset ever passed to SETBIT, not by how many bits are set. Using the raw 64-bit snowflake userId as that offset forces an allocation up to that huge number, and because snowflake ids are sparse — they can reach into the quintillions — a structure that's supposed to be one bit per online user becomes a near-empty, exabyte-scale allocation. The fix is to remap each userId to a small, dense index, say via a Redis INCR counter or a HASH from userId to index assigned on connect, and run SETBIT/GETBIT against that index instead. That keeps BITCOUNT semantics identical — we're still counting bits, only the offset's meaning changes. An alternative is sharding the bitmap by id range into keys like presence:online:<range>, though then the total count needs summing BITCOUNT across every shard with online users instead of one call. I'd verify by checking MEMORY USAGE scales with connected users, not the raw id magnitude, and that BITCOUNT still equals the real online count. I'd also flag that the mapping itself needs a consistent, cluster-wide lookup so it doesn't become a new bottleneck.
